# Cationic homopolymers inhibit spore and vegetative cell growth of Clostridioides difficile.

**Authors:** Joshua B. Jones; Lei Liu; Leslie A. Rank; Daniela Wetzel; Emily C. Woods; Naomi Biok; Sarah E. Anderson; Myung-ryul Lee; Runhui Liu; Sean Huth; Brindar K. Sandhu; Samuel H. Gellman; Shonna M. McBride

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Emory University School of Medicine, Emory Antibiotic Resistance Center, Atlanta, GA, USA | 2Department of Chemistry and Department of Medicine, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI, USA | 3Johnson & Johnson Inc., Skillman, NJ, USA | 4Department of Medicine, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA, USA | 5Department of Biology, Washington University, St. Louis, MO, USA | 6Department of Chemistry, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL, USA | 7State Key Laboratory of Bioreactor Engineering, School of Materials Science and Engineering, East China University of Science and Technology, Shanghai, China | 8Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA

## Abstract

A wide range of synthetic polymers have been explored for antimicrobial activity. These materials usually contain both cationic and hydrophobic subunits because these two characteristics are prominent among host-defense peptides. Here we describe a series of nylon-3 polymers containing only cationic subunits, and their evaluation against the gastrointestinal, spore-forming pathogen Clostridioides difficile. Despite their highly hydrophilic nature, these homopolymers showed efficacy against both the vegetative and spore forms of the bacterium, including an impact on C. difficile spore germination. The polymer designated P34 demonstrated the greatest efficacy against C. difficile strains, along with low propensities to lyse human red blood cells or intestinal epithelial cells. To gain insight into the mechanism of P34 action, we evaluated several cell-surface mutant strains of C. difficile to determine the impacts on growth, viability, and cell morphology. The results suggest that P34 interacts with the cell wall, resulting in severe cell bending and death in a concentration-dependent manner. The unexpected finding that nylon-3 polymers composed entirely of cationic subunits display significant activities toward C. difficile should expand the range of other polymers considered for antibacterial applications.

## Abstract

Clostridioides difficile is a spore-forming, anaerobic, and Gram-positive intestinal pathogen that causes life-threatening diarrhea.1–3 In the United States, nearly half a million people suffer from C. difficile infections (CDI), leading to 29,000 deaths annually.4 CDI is typically preceded by antibiotic-induced dysbiosis, which disrupts the colonic microbiota that provide colonization resistance against C. difficile.5, 6 C. difficile is easily transmitted as a spore, which is highly resistant to the effects of antibiotics or host antimicrobial compounds.7–12 Upon ingestion, C. difficile enters the gastrointestinal tract and produces two potent toxins, TcdA and TcdB, that can induce mild to severe diarrhea, pseudomembranous colitis, or toxic megacolon.13, 14 Antibiotic treatment options for C. difficile are limited, as the bacterium is resistant to a wide variety of antimicrobial drugs.15 Furthermore, the recurrence rate for CDI following treatment with the traditional antibiotic therapies (vancomycin, fidaxomicin, or metronidazole) can be as high as 20%, at which point fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is often recommended.4, 16–18 While FMT can be helpful in treating CDI, microbiota transplantation carries the risk of inadvertent transfer of additional life-threatening pathogens.19

Given the limitations of the current treatment options, there is a need for new antimicrobial agents that target both C. difficile vegetative cells and spores. A promising approach to achieve C. difficile cell death is to mimic the antimicrobial properties of host defense peptides using synthetic polymers. Relative to natural or synthetic peptides, polymers are easier to synthesize, and are less likely to be susceptible to proteolytic degradation.20–25

Prior work identified nylon-3 polymers (poly-β-amino acids) that mimic antimicrobial properties of host-defense peptides, including activity against a variety of bacteria and low propensity to damage mammalian cells (the latter property most commonly assessed via hemolysis assays).26,27 These polymers are prepared via anionic ring-opening polymerization of β-lactams.28 Natural host-defense peptides are highly diverse in terms of amino acid sequence, but large proportions of hydrophobic residues and cationic residues are a common feature in this class. Therefore, most synthetic polymers explored for antibacterial activity, including nylon-3 examples, have contained both hydrophobic and cationic subunits. The poly-β-amino acid backbone is similar to the backbone of natural proteins (which are poly-α-amino acids) in terms of physical properties, but the poly-β-amino acid backbone is highly resistant to proteolytic enzymes.28, 29 Thus, it is conceivable that a nylon-3 polymer active against C. difficile could be delivered orally and remain intact when it reached the site of infection, in the intestines.

We previously described a set of binary nylon-3 copolymers, containing both a hydrophobic and a cationic subunit, that displayed good activities toward C. difficile.25 Here we focus on new nylon-3 polymers that are composed entirely of cationic subunits. We investigated the minimal inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations of the homopolymers against C. difficile, as well as their effects on spore outgrowth and spore viability. We further analyzed actively growing C. difficile for morphological changes in the presence of polymers, and polymer impact on spore germination. The polymer designated P34 featured the best activity profile, including a low propensity to induce lysis of eukaryotic cells. Mutant strains of C. difficile with altered cell-surface properties were tested to assess potential targets of P34. The results suggest that P34 targets the vegetative cell and spore surfaces, causing defects in cell wall synthesis that lead to C. difficile death. Our findings demonstrate that polycationic polymers lacking subunits that are entirely hydrophobic deserve further attention as antibacterial agents.

## RESULTS

### Selection of cationic nylon-3 homopolymers

Our previous evaluation of nylon-3 polymers for activity toward C. difficile,25 based solely on MIC determinations, included two homopolymers that contained only cationic subunits in addition to 20 binary copolymers that contained both a cationic and a hydrophobic subunit. Both cationic homopolymers showed modest activity. We were surprised that polymers lacking a substantial complement of hydrophobic side chains would nevertheless hinder growth of C. difficile. This observation raised questions about the antibacterial mechanism of these homopolymers. In addition, this finding suggested interesting possibilities in terms of practical application, because highly cationic polymers are not expected to disrupt eukaryotic cell membranes but are predicted to be attracted to negatively charged bacterial cell surfaces.30

The studies reported here were motivated by the goal of identifying highly cationic nylon-3 polymers with improved activity against C. difficile, relative to the previous examples 25, and with low propensity to permeabilize human cells. One of the two cationic homopolymers, P21 from the previous study, was selected as a reference for experiments reported here (the other homopolymer was more hemolytic).39 This reference polymer is based on a nylon-3 subunit that contains only one side chain, with the composition - CH2NH3+ (protonation, leading to positive charge, expected at or near neutral pH). Two versions of this polymer, one with an average chain length of 10 subunits (P77) and the other with an average length of 20 subunits (P21), were included for evaluation (Figure 1).

Other cationic polymers were selected with the intent of addressing relationships between subunit structure and anti-C. difficile activities (Figure 1; and Figure S1A). One set of polymers could have a higher positive charge density relative to P21 and P77, because each subunit bears two basic groups in side chains rather than one. In P55 and P8 (average chain lengths of 10 and 20 subunits, respectively), both cationic groups are attached to a single side chain. The subunit in P27 and P34, on the other hand, presents two cationic groups from different side chains. For P55/P8 and P27/P34, it is possible that the high density of basic groups (two per subunit) causes some of the side chain amino groups to be unprotonated under our experimental conditions, to minimize repulsion among cationic groups. The difference in substitution patterns between the subunit of P55/P8 and the subunit of P27/P34 is likely to influence the conformational propensities of these subunits, and the resulting polymer chains may have different average shapes in solution.

A second set of polymers match P21/P77 in terms of charge density (one charge per subunit) but vary in other ways. P78 and P95 represent analogues of P21 in which subunit hydrophobicity is incrementally increased, via introduction of one saturated carbon per subunit in P78 or two saturated carbons per subunit in P95. In addition to the anticipated hydrophobicity changes, the subunits of P78 and P95 should have a different conformational propensity relative to the subunit in P21, because there are two substituents in P78 and P95, but only one in P21. P57 and P56 are analogues of P77 and P21, respectively, in which the separation between the cationic side chain group and the polymer backbone has been increased. However, side chain lengthening necessarily increases subunit hydrophobicity, because the atoms between the backbone and the cationic group in P57/P56 are nonpolar.

Each of the nylon-3 materials evaluated in these experiments can be categorized as a homopolymer because the subunits are identical in composition. However, each subunit has at least one stereogenic center in the backbone (some subunits have two), and therefore each subunit is chiral. All samples were prepared by ring-opening polymerization of a chiral β-lactam, but each β-lactam was used in racemic form. Therefore, each polymer has a random sequence of subunit absolute configurations along the chain; in other words, each polymer can be characterized as atactic or heterochiral.

### Cationic nylon-3 polymers exhibit variable effects on C. difficile viability

We assessed the efficacy of the cationic nylon-3 polymers against vegetative cells and spores of C. difficile strain 630Δerm by determining the ability of each polymer to prevent vegetative cell growth (MIC), kill bacterial cells (MBC), prevent spore outgrowth into vegetative cells (OIC), and inactivate spores (SIC), as previously described25 (Table 2). Incubation of most polymers with vegetative cells prevented cell growth, with MIC values in the range 12.5-100 μg/mL; only P77 had an MIC value >100 μg/mL (Table 2). Inactivation of vegetative cells (MBC) was generally achieved in the range 50-100 μg/mL; only P77 had an MBC value >100 μg/mL and P95 of 25 μg/mL. All polymers inhibited spore outgrowth, with OIC values in the range 6.25-50 μg/mL. Most had OIC values of 12.5 or 25 μg/mL, which was considered practical for potential therapeutic use. Spore inhibition (SIC) was achieved only by polymers P57, P77 and P95 at concentrations of 50-100 μg/mL. There is no obvious explanation for these activities based on inspection of the subunits of these polymers. These results suggest that the spore outgrowth inhibition arises from effects exerted on cells during the transition from a spore to a vegetative cell or during subsequent vegetative cell growth.

Among the polymer variants, P95 had the greatest efficacy against C. difficile, demonstrating improved inhibition and killing of vegetative cells, as well as improved activity against outgrowing spores relative to the other polymers. However, as discussed below, P95 was more hemolytic than most of the other polymers (Figure 2). The most active polymers generally had an average of 20 subunits per chain; decreased average chain length either led to a small diminution in activity, as was most evident in MIC values, or caused no change in efficacy.

### Polymer effects on red blood cells and intestinal epithelial cells

Selective disruption of prokaryotic vs. eukaryotic cells would presumably minimize toxic side effects of such polymers in vivo. We used a common measurement, involving the ability to lyse human red blood cells, to evaluate the ability of the cationic nylon-3 polymers to disrupt eukaryotic membranes (Figure 2A; Table 2). Most of the polymers exerted little effect on red blood cells, with <10% hemolysis detected at 500 μg/mL polymer (i.e., HC10 > 500 μg/mL). A greater propensity for hemolysis was observed for P78 (HC10 = 125 μg/mL), and still greater for P95 (HC10 = 31 μg/mL). Across the series P21, P78 and P95, the incremental increase in subunit hydrophobicity seems to correlate with a rise in hemolytic activity.

We undertook a second type of measurement to assess polymer effects on human cells by evaluating toxicity toward Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells (Figure 2B; Table 2). Since C. difficile causes disease by colonizing the intestines, results from this assay might be more relevant to potential applications of nylon-3 polymers than results of hemolysis studies. All 10 of the cationic nylon-3 polymers displayed very low toxicity toward Caco-2 cells, with IC10 ≥ 500 μg/mL.

Among the 10 polymers, P34 appeared to exhibit the best combination of properties. P34 was among the most effective in terms of little or no propensity to lyse red blood cells (HC10 > 500 μg/mL) or kill Caco-2 cells (IC10 = 500 μg/mL), and P34 displayed good vegetative cell growth inhibition (MIC = 25 μg/mL), bactericidal effects (MBC = 50 μg/mL), and inhibition of spore outgrowth (OIC = 25 μg/mL) (Figure 2A and 2B; Table 2). These results led us to focus on P34 for subsequent studies, although selected other polymers were examined as well. Polymer P34 was further tested against evolutionarily diverse C. difficile strains and showed significant activity against vegetative cells and spores of C. difficile strains R20291 and M120 (Table 3).

### Polymer P34 and other cationic polymers alter C. difficile morphology.

As relatively large molecules with high positive charge density, the polymers would be predicted to interact with the bacterial cell surface, where they could cause growth inhibition by interfering with cell wall synthesis or stability. To test this hypothesis, we examined the morphology of C. difficile vegetative cells that were grown in the presence of each polymer at concentrations representing half of the MIC value for that polymer (0.5xMIC). As illustrated in Figure 3, several polymers dramatically affected the morphology of vegetative cells, resulting in cell swelling and curling. The most striking morphological impacts were observed with polymers P34 and P27, which are comprised of the same monomer but have average lengths of 20- and 10-mer, respectively. Among the ten polymers we examined, P34 and P27 induced the most severe cell bending. This effect was qualitatively similar to the effect of vancomycin on C. difficile. Vancomycin is known to interrupt bacterial cell wall synthesis; thus, the behavior we observed for P27 and P34 suggests that these polymers, too, may exert an impact on C. difficile cell wall synthesis. Given that each repeating unit for P34 and P27 has two ammonium groups (Figure 1), we hypothesized that the high positive charge density could contribute to the severe vegetative cell bending. To test this hypothesis, we evaluated the cell bending caused by polymers P8 and P55, which also have two ammonium groups per subunit, but with a different subunit structure relative to that of P27 and P34 (Figure 1). The microscopic observations for P8 and P55 suggest that these polymers cause less severe cell bending relative to P27 and P34 (Figure 3). Further, P21, a polymer with only one ammonium group per subunit, caused cell bending comparable to that caused by P27 and P34. These observations suggest that high positive charge density alone does not explain the severe bending of C. difficile vegetative cells observed with some of the nylon-3 polymers we evaluated. We speculate that the conformational propensities of the polymer chains may be important as well.

### Cationic polymers have varying impacts on C. difficile spore germination

Because of the observed effects of the cationic nylon-3 polymers on spore viability (Table 2), we assessed the abilities of these polymers to interfere with C. difficile spore germination. Purified spores of strain 630Δerm were heat-activated,40 and incubated with individual polymers at their respective outgrowth inhibitory concentration (OIC, Table 2), prior to the addition of the germinant taurocholate (TA). Germination efficiency was assessed as the change in optical density over time (Figure 4; and Figure S2). For polymers P8 and P55 (two cationic charges per subunit), no significant differences between the control and samples treated with polymers and germinant were observed (Figure 4A). However, spores that were treated with polymer P55 in the absence of germinant demonstrated a greater change in optical density, which led us to wonder whether this polymer might function as a spore germinant. Similar but more pronounced effects were observed when P55 was applied to the spores at 2x OIC (Figure S2C). However, further analysis of germination, using phase-contrast microscopy of spores exposed for 30 min to P55 at 1x OIC, did not reveal induced spore germination by P55 compared to the non-treated sample (data not shown). Thus, the loss in optical density observed with P55 appears to be an aberrant spectrophotometric effect. P27 generated a lag in spore germination when taurocholate was present, but no difference in the final germination measurement was observed (Figure 4B). P57 elicited a significantly reduced germination rate (P ≤ 0.05) compared to the control (Figure 4C). These data suggest that polymer P57 can interfere with germination, likely by interfering with germinant binding.

Polymer P21, with a single positive charge per subunit, produced a short lag in spore germination (P ≤ 0.05; Figure S2A). Polymers P78 and P95, with related subunit structures but additional nonpolar side chains (methyl or ethyl, respectively), had no impact on spore germination, with or without taurocholate (Figure S2B). Overall, these data show that variations in polymer subunit structure can lead to significant variations in the effects exerted by these polymers on C. difficile spores. These effects are not correlated with any single parameter; such as charge density or average chain length. The data suggest that some of these polymers have some capacity to hinder spore germination in the presence of taurocholate, although the mechanism by which this occurs is not understood.

### Polymer P34 decreases the growth rate of 630Δerm and cell surface mutants, but has little effect on an ldt1 mutant

We evaluated diverse surface mutant strains of C. difficile to investigate potential surface targets for polymer P34.41 The individual null mutants tested were in dltD, which increases cell surface density and positive charge through the D-alanylation of teichoic acid,42, 43 sigV, which regulates dlt and genes involved in the deacetylation of peptidoglycan,34, 38, 44 ldt1, which induces 3-3 cross-links in peptidoglycan,45 vanZ1, which confers teicoplanin resistance,35 and blaD, which encodes a β-lactamase conferring ampicillin (β-lactam) resistance in C. difficile.36 Polymer P34 was incubated with exponentially growing cells of C. difficile 630Δerm and the cell surface mutant strains at a sub-lethal concentration of 0.35x MIC to assess differences in growth in the presence of the polymer, which could implicate specific surface features as targets of the polymer (Figure S3). No differences in growth among the surface mutants and the parent strain in MHB medium only were observed (data not shown). As expected, growth of the parent strain at sub-MIC concentrations of polymer P34 was stunted relative to growth in MHB alone (Figure S3). The growth rate of the cell surface mutant strains sigV, dltD, blaD, and vanZ1 were similar to the wild type strain when exposed to P34. However, the ltd1 mutant acclimated significantly faster than the parent strain in the presence of P34 (P ≤ 0.05) (Figure S3).

### Bactericidal activity of polymer P34 is concentration-dependent

Time-kill assays were performed to determine if polymer P34 has concentration-dependent or time-dependent effects on C. difficile cells. Vegetative cells of 630Δerm and the ldt1 mutant strain were grown to exponential phase and treated with P34 or a control antimicrobial agent, metronidazole or vancomycin, at 8x MIC levels, respectively (Figure 5). The ldt1 mutant was included in this experiment because it appeared to be less affected by sub-MIC P34 concentrations relative to other mutants (Figure S3). The number of colony-forming units (CFU) was determined at regular intervals following polymer exposure (Figure 5). Metronidazole and vancomycin exhibited concentration and time-dependent effects on C. difficile, respectively, that were consistent with previous reports (Figure 5). Exposure to polymer P34 caused a reduction of viable cells to below the limit of detection within four hours for the parent strain and within two hours for the ldt1 mutant strain. Although the ldt1 mutant seemed to be more sensitive than the parent strain to P34 at 8x MIC, this effect was not statistically significant (P ≥ 0.05). Polymer P34 reduced the number of viable C. difficile cells rapidly and dramatically after exposure. These results demonstrate that polymer P34 acts in a concentration-dependent manner, similar to metronidazole, rather than by a time-dependent mechanism, as observed for vancomycin.

## DISCUSSION

Antibiotics should ideally display high antimicrobial potency, low toxicity toward host cells, stability toward chemical and biological degradation, low production costs, and little tendency for the development of resistance.46–48 Synthetic polymers have the potential to satisfy all of these criteria. The survey of cationic nylon-3 polymers described here reveals that this polymer family can display meaningful inhibitory activity toward the recalcitrant human pathogen C. difficile, along with other favorable properties.

Potency toward C. difficile and selectivity (as indicated by a lack of deleterious effects on eukaryotic cells) of the polymers we examined vary as a function of chemical structure. Structural variables among our polymer set included chain length, subunit structure and positive charge density. Most of these cationic polymers had similar impacts on C. difficile spores, but greater variability was observed against the vegetative form. The most promising polymer, P34, exhibited good activity against multiple C. difficile strains and low toxicity toward human cells (Table 2). Activity differences between P34 and other members of our polymer set offer insights on the features of P34 that are most important for activity against C. difficile.

For antimicrobial polymers and surfaces, a high positive charge density is generally beneficial for biocidal efficacy.49–51 However, variation between one positive charge per subunit or two positive charges per subunit did not lead to consistent activity variations among our polymers. Thus, polymers that potentially have two charges per subunit (P8/P55 and P27/P34) did not display any bactericidal or sporicidal advantage relative to polymers with one charge per subunit (P21/P77, P56/P57, P78 and P95). As noted above, it is possible that P8/P55 and/or P27/P34 would not be fully protonated, to minimize internal charge repulsion. In addition, the presence of sulfur in the side chains of P8/P55 and P56/P57 had no effect, as judged by comparisons with polymers lacking sulfur in the side chains. An average chain length of 20 subunits seemed to be favorable relative to an average length of 10 subunits in terms of efficacy against vegetative cells. Increasing polymer chain length has been shown to increase hemolytic activity in other polymer families;47, 52 based on these precedents, we focused on nylon-3 polymers that had average length no greater than 20 subunits to minimize hemolytic activity.

The results of previous studies suggested that antimicrobial polymers are most effective if they contain two types of subunit, one bearing a positive charge, to cause polymer adsorption to the bacterial cell surface, and another that is purely hydrophobic, to cause insertion into and disruption of the bacterial membrane.47, 53–55 In contrast, none of the homopolymers we investigated contained a purely hydrophobic subunit. Thus, our findings lead to the unexpected conclusion that it is not necessary to combine cationic and purely hydrophobic subunits for activity against C. difficile.

Within our polymer set, comparisons suggest that increasing hydrophobicity within the cationic subunit has at most only a modest effect on MIC activity toward C. difficile. For example, the subunits in P21, P78 and P95 become incrementally more hydrophobic, because the number of side-chain CH2 groups increases incrementally across this series, but P21 and P78 displayed similar MIC values. P95 exhibited improved efficacy against C. difficile (Table 2) relative to P21 and P78, but the increased hydrophobicity of the P95 subunit also correlated with a dramatic increase in hemolytic activity. Increased hydrophobicity seems generally to lead to increased lysis of red blood cells,47, 56, 57 and the high hemolytic activity of P95 suggests that once a certain threshold of hydrophobicity is reached, even a high positive charge density cannot suppress lysis of eukaryotic cell membranes. Most of the cationic polymers we examined were notably less hemolytic than the natural peptide LL-37 or a synthetic magainin 2 analogue.25, 58

For spore germination (OIC), no clear correlation was found between chain length, charge density or subunit structure. The most effective polymers at preventing growth (lowest OIC values), P78 and P95, exhibited no obvious impact on spore germination in the presence or absence of germinant. In contrast to results previously obtained with nylon-3 co-polymers containing both cationic and purely hydrophobic subunits, which did not impact germination,25 some of the cationic nylon-3 polymers studied here influenced the germination process. Specifically, polymer P57 reduced germination rate, while P27 and P21 caused delays in spore germination in the presence of germinant (Figure 4; Figure S2). These polymers may interact with the outermost spore layers to compete for access to the germinant receptors, but further investigation is needed to determine the specific mechanisms of these interactions.

Only a few studies have investigated the effects of primarily cationic peptides on Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, and varying behavior has been observed.59–64 Polycationic polymers are expected to be largely hydrophilic rather than amphiphilic, and it has been suggested that polycations act via a mechanism that does not involve the disturbance of lipid bilayers.39 However, Epand et al. showed that a cationic nylon-3 polymer could induce segregation of anionic lipids in a bilayer, leading to phase-boundary defects that could cause leakage.65 Hovakeemian et al. demonstrated that the purely cationic polymer P21 induces leakage from vesicles derived from fungal lipids by electrostatically driven polymer-lipid clustering.66 Very few studies have investigated morphological changes of Gram-positive bacteria when exposed to cationic homopolymers. A leucine-based cationic homopolymer was effective against B. subtilis, but exerted no obvious effects on cell morphology,67 while the cationic and hydrophilic polymer P4MVP28 had no discernible morphological impact on and was not bactericidal toward S. aureus.60

We observed severe cell bending of C. difficile when exposed to some cationic nylon-3 polymers, with some darker cells, suggesting the loss of cell wall integrity and water intrusion (Figure 3). The morphological effects were most prominent for polymers P34 and P27, which exerted effects that were comparable to those exerted by vancomycin. P34 and P27 have two positive charges per subunit, but this feature is not sufficient for pronounced cell bending, because neither P8 nor P55, which also have two positive charges per subunit, induced the severe bending observed with P34 and P27. Moreover, P21, which contains one positive charge per subunit, caused significant cell bending.

Vancomycin inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding to and sequestering the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan.68 Based on the similar morphological effects of polymer P34 and vancomycin, we propose that P34 also impacts cell wall synthesis. Cationic polymers do not necessarily interact with specific cell-surface proteins, as previously shown for interactions of P21 with fungal membranes,66 and this feature lessens the probability of the development of resistance via a single mechanism.

We detected improved growth of the ldt1 mutant at sub-MIC concentrations of polymer P34, suggesting that cell wall crosslinking differences in the mutant could impact polymer efficacy. The Ldtcd1 (ldt1) gene encodes for one out of three L,D-transpeptidases in the C. difficile genome.69 The peptidoglycan structure of C. difficile is unusual, as it contains up to 70% 3-3 cross-links, which are generated by L,D-transpeptidases.45, 69 The inactivation of Ldtcd1 caused a ~50% reduction of 3-3 cross-links and ~4% of 4-3 cross-links compared to the parental strain, resulting in a marked decrease in cross-linked peptidoglycan.45 However, using higher concentrations (8x MIC), the ldt1 mutant had a tendency to die more quickly compared to the parent strain. The underlying mechanism that results in the phenotype of the ldt1 mutant under diverse concentrations of the polymer is not understood. Other mutants with cell surface defects were tested and did not differ substantially in their responses to P34, however the possibility remains that other surface properties not tested could be important for polymer effects, including spore coat proteins and peptidoglycan deacetylases.70, 71

The efficacy of nylon-3 homopolymer P34 against C. difficile vegetative cells and spores, combined with the low toxicity toward eukaryotic cells and a mechanism of action exerted at the C. difficile cell surface, make this polymer an attractive candidate for therapeutic applications to combat C. difficile infections. Future studies will probe the in vivo tolerance and bioavailability of polymer P34, as well as the efficacy of P34 in an animal model of C. difficile infection.

## METHODS

### Bacterial strains and growth conditions

Table 1 lists the bacterial strains and plasmids used in this study. An anaerobic chamber (Coy Laboratory Products) was used to grow C. difficile strains at 37°C in an atmosphere of 10% H2, 5% CO2, and 85% N2.72, 73 Bacteria were grown in Brain Heart Infusion media (BD Difco) supplemented with 0.5% yeast extract (BHIS), Mueller-Hinton Broth (MHB; BD Difco), 70:30 sporulation agar74, or BHIS agar supplemented with 0.1% taurocholic acid (Millipore Sigma) for spore germination.74, 75 As needed, C. difficile vegetative cells or spores were grown in the presence of polymer or antibiotics (Sigma-Aldrich) at the concentrations stated in the text.

### Synthesis and characterization of monomers and cationic nylon-3 polymers

The β-lactam monomers were prepared by the reactions of chlorosulfonyl isocyanate (CSI) with alkenes. The β-lactam monomers for P21/P7739 and P7876 have been reported previously. The synthesis of the β-lactam monomer for P95 is reported elsewhere.77 The synthetic protocols for the β-lactam monomers for P8, P34 and P56 are described in the supporting information (supporting information Scheme S1, S2 and S3; Figures S4–S12). Each β-lactam was generated as a racemic mixture, and the resulting polymers were heterochiral.

Cationic nylon-3 polymers were synthesized using the previously published method of anionic ring-opening polymerization of β-lactam monomers28 (Figure S1B). These reactions were conducted in a N2-purged glovebox that kept the moisture level below 0.5 ppm. The β-lactam to be polymerized was dissolved in either THF or DMAc. The polymerization reaction was initiated by the addition of the co-initiator (p-tert-butylbenzoyl chloride) in a specific molar proportion relative to the β-lactam concentration. This proportion was chosen based on the desired average polymer chain length; for example, 0.05 mol% co-initiator was used if the intended average chain length was 20 subunits. After the co-initiator had been added, lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (2.5 equivalents relative to p-tert-butylbenzoyl chloride) was added. The reaction solution was stirred overnight at room temperature and then removed from the glovebox and quenched by addition of a few drops of methanol. At this point, the polymer chain contained Boc protecting groups on side-chain nitrogens; this material was dissolved in THF (regardless of polymerization reaction solvent) and precipitated by addition of pentane; this process was repeated three times. Side-chain protected polymers were dried to constant weight under vacuum and then subjected to gel permeation chromatography (GPC) using THF or DMAc as the mobile phase for determination of dispersity (Đ), number average molecular weight (Mn) and average polymer chain length (DP GPC). Side-chain protecting groups were removed by addition of 3 mL trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and 5% (v/v) triisopropylsilane (TIPS). The resulting solutions were stirred for 2 hours at room temperature, and the deprotected nylon-3 polymers were isolated by precipitation with cold diethyl ether. Polymer samples were dried under vacuum to constant weight, dissolved in ~5 mL Millipore water and lyophilized to yield polymers as TFA salts. These polymers were subjected to proton nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H NMR) for determination of average chain length (DP NMR). GPC and NMR characterization results for the cationic polymers in this study are available in the supporting information (Figures S13–S31).

### Hemolysis assays

Hemolytic activity of polymers was evaluated using human red blood cells (RBCs) as previously described.25, 27, 78 Briefly, 100 μL of 2% RBC suspension in TBS (Tris-Buffered Saline, pH 7.2) was treated with an equivalent volume of polymer solution in a 2-fold dilution series in TBS ranging from 500 to 3.9 μg/mL in a 96-well plate for 1 h at 37°C. RBC treated with TBS only (without polymer) and RBC treated with Triton X-100 (20% (v/v) Triton X-100 in TBS) were incorporated as “blank” and positive control, respectively. After centrifugation at 3200 x g for 5 minutes, 80 μL of the supernatant from each well was transferred to a new 96-well plate, and the optical density (OD) of the supernatant was measured at 405 nm using a plate reader. Hemolysis was calculated using the equation (% hemolysis = (A405polymer − A405blank)/(A405pos.control − A405blank) × 100) and plotted against the polymer concentration. The HC10 value is the polymer concentration required to lyse 10% of RBCs.

### Caco-2 cell toxicity assays

Polymer toxicity was evaluated using human intestinal epithelial Caco-2 cells and the CytoTox-ONE assay kit (Promega), which measures the release of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) from membrane-damaged cells, as previously described.27 Briefly, approximately 1 × 104 cells in DMEM medium, containing 10% serum and other nutrients, were seeded in each well of a 96-well plate, which was incubated for 72 h at 37°C. Medium was exchanged for fresh DMEM (phenol red- and pyruvate-free) shortly before the assay was performed. Cells were treated with polymers at varied concentrations in a 2-fold serial dilution series ranging from 500 to 3.9 μg/mL for 6 h at 37°C. The cells in each well were then analyzed using the CytoTox-ONE assay kit. Caco-2 cells in DMEM only (without polymer) and cells treated with lysate solution to cause 100% release of LDH (10% Triton-X 100) were incorporated as the “blank” and positive control, respectively. Fluorescence intensity was measured on a microplate reader using ex/em 560/590 nm. Cell death was calculated using (% cell death = (Fpolymer − Fblank)/(Fpos.control − Fblank) × 100) and plotted against the polymer concentration. The IC10 value represents the polymer concentration needed to cause 10% cell death.

### Spore preparation and quantification

Spores were purified as previously described with some modifications 79. C. difficile strains were grown on 70:30 sporulation agar for 48 h, removed from the anaerobic chamber, and kept outside of the chamber in atmospheric oxygen overnight to encourage the lysis of vegetative cells. Cells were then scraped from the plates, resuspended in sterile water, and frozen at −80°C. After thawing, spore preparations were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 3200 × g, the supernatant discarded, and the pellet resuspended in 1 mL of PBS + 1% BSA (spore buffer). The suspension was then applied to a 12 mL column of 50% sucrose and centrifuged at 3200 x g in a swing bucket rotor for 20 minutes. The supernatant was removed, and the spores were checked for < 5% cell debris using phase contrast microscopy 80. This process was repeated until cell debris was sufficiently removed. Finally, spore pellets were washed three times with spore buffer and resuspended for enumeration.

Spores were enumerated by performing serial dilutions of the initial spore stock in spore buffer. Spore dilutions were then incubated at 55°C for 20 minutes and plated on reduced BHIS agar supplemented with 0.1% taurocholic acid 75. Purified spore stocks were adjusted to a concentration of 5 x 106 CFU/mL for Outgrowth Inhibitory (OIC) and Sporicidal Inhibitory Concentration (SIC) experiments.

### Determination of Minimal Inhibitory (MIC) and Minimal Bactericidal (MBC) Concentrations

Minimal Inhibitory Concentration experiments were performed as previously described 25. Briefly, cultures were grown in MHB to log-phase (OD600 of 0.45), diluted 1:10 in MHB and 15 μL added to wells of a pre-reduced 96-well U-bottom plate containing 135 μL of MHB with two-fold dilutions of polymer or antibiotic. Negative controls containing MHB only and positive controls containing MHB only and cell culture were also included. After 24 h of incubation, wells were checked for colony growth. The assay was performed at least three times with biologically independent replicates for each strain, and the MIC was recorded as the lowest concentration at which no bacterial growth was observable.

Minimal Bactericidal Concentration experiments were performed concurrently with MIC assays. Wells from the MIC assays that did not have observable growth were added to a microcentrifuge tube containing BHIS only and incubated at 37°C for 24 h. Following incubation, cultures were checked for bacterial growth. This assay was performed at least three times with biologically independent replicates for each strain, and the lowest concentration at which there was no visible bacterial growth was recorded as MBC.

### Determination of Outgrowth Inhibitory (OIC) and Spore Inhibitory (SIC) Concentrations

Outgrowth Inhibitory Concentration experiments were performed as previously described, 25 with minor modifications. Purified spores were used to avoid cell debris that could potentially bind the polymer and impact OICs. Spores were purified using 50% sucrose as described above and added to a final concentration of 5 x 106 CFU/mL to wells of a pre-reduced 96-well U-bottom plate containing 135 μL of MHB with 0.1% taurocholate and two-fold dilutions of polymer or antibiotic. Negative controls containing only MHB, along with positive controls containing MHB and cell culture were included. After 24 h incubation, wells were checked for bacterial growth. The OIC was recorded as the lowest concentration at which no bacterial growth was observed.

Spore Inhibitory Concentration experiments were performed concurrently with OIC assays, as previously described.25 Spores from wells in the OIC assays that did not have observable growth were diluted 1:10 in a microcentrifuge tube containing BHIS with 0.1% taurocholate and incubated at 37°C for 24 h. The lowest concentration with no visible bacterial growth was recorded as the SIC.

### Germination Assays

Spores were purified as described in Spore preparation and quantification. The spore pellets were then washed three times with spore buffer and resuspended to an OD600 = 3.0. Germination assays were carried out as previously described40, 81 After treatment of spores for 30 min at 60°C to stimulate germination, spore germination was performed in BHIS broth containing 5 mM taurocholic acid (TA) and the concentration of polymers at their respective OIC (Table 2). Spores were allowed to incubate with the polymer for five minutes prior to the addition of TA. The OD600 was determined immediately and every two minutes during incubation at room temperature. Results are presented as means and standard errors of the means of three independent biological replicates.

### Vegetative cell growth assays

The effects of sub-MIC concentrations of polymers on growth of C. difficile were assessed as previously described with minor modifications.82 Cell cultures were grown in MHB at 37°C in an anaerobic chamber to logarithmic phase (OD600 of 0.50). Cultures were then diluted in MHB or MHB containing 0.35x MIC (8.75 μg/mL) of polymer P34 to a starting OD600 of 0.02 and incubated for 8 h. Cultures were sampled every hour and the OD600 was measured.

### Measurement of polymer killing rate on vegetative cells

Time-kill curves were performed as previously described with slight modifications.83 C. difficile were grown in MHB to exponential phase and diluted to an OD600 of 0.10. This culture was combined with MHB or MHB containing polymer or antibiotics at an 8x MIC to achieve a starting cell concentration of approximately 1.0x107 CFU/mL. Serial dilutions in BHIS were prepared from each sample at regular time points, plated on BHIS agar with 0.1% taurocholate, and incubated anaerobically at 37°C for 24 h. Colonies were counted and the number of surviving cells calculated. Cultures containing bacterial strains without any polymer or antibiotic were used as controls.

### Phase Contrast Microscopy

Following MIC experiments, C. difficile cultures representing the highest concentration that supported growth (0.5x MIC) were removed, pelleted, and assessed by phase contrast microscopy as previously described.80 Briefly, 2 μL of pelleted cells were placed on a 0.7% agarose pad, visualized and captured using phase-contrast with a 100x oil immersion objective, microscope, and camera (Nikon).
